system_overview: This specification models the basic thermocycling process of Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR), a biochemical technique used to amplify a specific segment of DNA. PCR works by repeatedly cycling through three temperature-dependent phases: denaturation (high heat separates double-stranded DNA into single-stranded templates), annealing (cooling allows short primer sequences to bind to complementary sites on the templates, forming primer-template hybrids), and extension (at medium temperature, a polymerase enzyme extends the hybrids into new double-stranded DNA). Each cycle approximately doubles the amount of DNA, producing exponential growth that eventually follows an S-curve as primers are depleted.
actors_and_components: The system has no concurrent actors. It models a single reaction vessel undergoing temperature cycling. The key molecular components tracked are: double-stranded DNA molecules, single-stranded template molecules, short primer molecules, and primer-template hybrid molecules.
state_variables: The system tracks five quantities: (1) the current temperature phase, which cycles through three levels representing extension temperature, denaturation temperature, and an intermediate cooling step; (2) the count of available primer molecules; (3) the count of double-stranded DNA molecules; (4) the count of single-stranded template molecules; (5) the count of primer-template hybrid molecules.
initial_state: The temperature is at the extension level. The primer count equals a constant representing the initial primer stock. The DNA count equals a constant representing the initial DNA stock. There are no templates and no hybrids, since all DNA starts in double-stranded form.
actions: Four actions model the PCR cycle: (1) Heating: raises temperature from extension level to denaturation level. All double-stranded DNA and hybrids are denatured into single-stranded templates. Primers from denatured hybrids are recovered. (2) Cooling: lowers temperature from denaturation level to extension level. No molecular changes occur. (3) Annealing: lowers temperature from extension level to the annealing level. A nondeterministically chosen number of primers bind to available templates, consuming both and producing that many hybrids. The number bound is between 1 and the minimum of available primers and templates. (4) Extension: raises temperature from annealing level to extension level. All hybrids are converted to double-stranded DNA.
safety_properties: Primer counts are always non-negative. Conservation of molecular material: the total count of templates plus primers plus twice the count of double-stranded DNA and hybrids remains constant throughout all transitions, equaling the initial primer stock plus twice the initial DNA stock.
liveness_properties: NOT_SPECIFIED. A primer depletion property (eventually all primers are consumed) is defined but explicitly noted as not holding in general, because the system can stutter or cycle without consuming all primers.
model_bounds: The initial DNA count and initial primer count are declared as constants. For model checking, typical values are 5 for each.
additional_assumptions: The specification abstracts from many biological details: nucleotide supply is assumed unlimited, primer binding is nondeterministic (any number up to the available minimum may bind in a single annealing step), DNA re-annealing during cooling is neglected, and extension is assumed to complete for all available hybrids. Two types of primers are required in real PCR but the specification does not distinguish between them. No fairness assumptions are made on the temperature cycling, so the system may stutter indefinitely.
